uncited: Unlike standard fixed-step ray marching, which samples at uniform intervals regardless of scene content, optimized methods advance the ray analytically from one cell boundary to the next, minimizing floating-point operations and redundant samples [S5, S7, unofficial].
This family builds on [Ray-grid traversal](17-ray-grid-traversal.md) by focusing on the efficiency of the traversal loop and the integration of sampling strategies.
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of advancing analytically from one cell boundary to the next, avoiding fixed-distance sampling steps [S5][S7, unofficial].
The algorithm determines the next cell by comparing the distances to the upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].
**Step Direction ($\text{step}_i$):** Determines the index increment direction [S4, unofficial].
If $d_i = 0$, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity [S5].
**Time/Distance Delta ($\Delta t_i$ or $s_{\Delta i}$):** The distance along the ray to traverse one voxel width [S2, unofficial][S5].
where $v_i$ is the voxel size and $\widehat{d}_i$ is the unit direction component [S2, unofficial][S5].
**Time/Distance to Next Boundary ($t_{max, i}$ or $s_{max, i}$):** The distance from the ray origin to the first boundary crossed in axis $i$ [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].
The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index [S3, unofficial].
If the ray starts inside the grid, the initial boundary is the next one in the direction of travel [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].
Identify the axis $k$ with the minimum boundary distance: $t_{min} = \min(t_{max, x}, t_{max, y}, t_{max, z})$ [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].
Advance the index in axis $k$: $\text{index}_k \leftarrow \text{index}_k + \text{step}_k$ [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].
Update the boundary distance for axis $k$: $t_{max, k} \leftarrow t_{max, k} + \Delta t_k$ [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5].

When the ray crosses an edge or corner (i.e., two or three $t_{max}$ values are equal), the traversal must advance all corresponding axes to maintain 4-connectivity (or 6/8-connectivity in 2D/3D) and avoid zero-length segments [S5].
The implementation uses independent `if` checks for ties rather than `if/elif` chains [S5].
A tie tolerance $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DDA}}$ is used to handle floating-point drift, typically defined as $64 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}} \max(1 \text{ cm}, L_{\mathrm{grid}})$ [S5].

Originating from the need to accelerate volume rendering in medical imaging and real-time applications, ray marching optimization evolved from basic Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal [S5, S7, unofficial].
